steps.label: What valence is
lines: Valence is the combining capacity of an
For the representative elements it equals the
number of outermost electrons, or eight minus
steps.why: The two rules cover both halves of a period: metals use their few outer electrons directly, while non-metals combine through the electrons they lack from eight.
common_mistakes: Giving only the outermost-electrons rule. For non-metals the working rule is eight minus that number.
Confusing valence with the number of shells.
steps.memory_tip: Count the outer electrons; if the count passes four, count what is missing from eight instead.
steps.margin_note: Both rules must appear; the period trend below uses them.

steps.label: Across a period
lines: Across a period the number of outer
electrons rises from 1 to 8, so the valence
with respect to hydrogen rises from 1 to 4

steps.why: The hydride formulas make the rise-and-fall visible: up to silicon the outer electrons set the valence, after silicon the missing-from-eight count takes over and the valence falls.
common_mistakes: Writing that valence rises continuously across a period. With hydrogen it peaks at 4 (silicon) and falls back to 1.
Mixing the two series: the 1-to-7 rise belongs to the oxides, the 1-4-1 pattern to the hydrides.
steps.memory_tip: Read the valence straight off the hydride formulas: one H, two H, three H, four H, then three, two, one.
steps.margin_note: The formula line is the evidence; both marks sit on this trend with its examples.

steps.label: Down a group

lines.text: Down a group the valence stays the same

lines: All the elements of a group have the same
number of outermost electrons, so their
Example: Li, Na and K each show valence 1.
steps.why: Valence depends only on the outer-shell electron count, and going down a group changes the number of shells but not that count — so the valence is constant.
common_mistakes: Writing that valence increases down a group because the atom grows. Size changes; the outer electron count does not.
steps.memory_tip: Down a group only the shell count changes; the outer electron count, and so the valence, stays fixed.
steps.margin_note: One boxed line with the same-outer-electrons reason closes the answer.
